facts.statement: Fossils of Australodocus bohetii were recovered in 1909 from the Upper Dinosaur Member of the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania.
facts.quote: The remains of Australodocus bohetii were recovered in 1909 from the Upper Dinosaur Member of the Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania

facts.statement: The original series of four vertebrae collected in 1909 was reduced to two surviving pieces after the others were destroyed during World War II.
facts.quote: These vertebrae were originally part of a series of four vertebrae collected in the 1909 expedition led by Werner Janensch; like some other fossils collected by German expeditions to Africa, the other bones were destroyed in World War II.

facts.statement: While initially classified as a diplodocid, recent analyses suggest Australodocus may instead belong to the titanosauriform clade.
facts.quote: Though initially considered a diplodocid, recent analyses suggest it may instead be a titanosauriform.

facts.statement: Studies by John Whitlock and colleagues found Australodocus to be a member of the Titanosauriformes clade, possibly closely related to Brachiosaurus.
facts.quote: However, several later studies by John Whitlock and colleagues found that Australodocus is actually a member of the sauropod clade Titanosauriformes, possibly closely related to Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: Tschopp et al. (2015) recovered Australodocus as a diplodocine diplodocid related to Supersaurus, but noted this placement was untenable due to its shared somphospondylous internal structure with titanosauriforms.
facts.quote: Tschopp et al. (2015) recovered Australodocus as a diplodocine diplodocid, closely related to Supersaurus and Dinheirosaurus (which may be a synonym of the former), but stressed that the low number of titanosauriform taxa used in the cladistic analysis made such a placement untenable due to the shared somphospondylous internal structure of Australodocus and somphospondylian titanosauriforms.

facts.statement: Mannion et al. (2019) classified Australodocus as a non-titanosaur somphospondyl and considered it a potential euhelopodid based on cervical internal structure.
facts.quote: Mannion et al.(2019) found Australodocus to be a non-titanosaur somphospondyl based on the somphospondylous nature of the internal structure of the cervicals, considering it a potential euhelopodid.

facts.statement: Australodocus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 147 million years ago in the Tithonian stage, in what is now Africa.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente 147 millones de años, durante el Titoniense, en lo que hoy es África.

facts.statement: Australodocus had a shorter neck than other sauropods because its vertebrae were shorter than those of its counterparts and possessed a bifurcate neural spine.
facts.quote: Australodocus poseía un cuello más corto que otros saurópodos debido a que las vértebras eran más cortas que la de sus contrapartes además estas poseían una espina neural bifurcada.

facts.statement: Australodocus reached an estimated length of 25.00 meters, a height of 7.00 meters, and a weight of 12 tons.
facts.quote: Llegaría a medir 25,00 metros de largo y 7,00 de alto y un peso estimado de 12 toneladas.

facts.statement: The time range for Australodocus is estimated from 149.2 to 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Tithonian to Tithonian (149.2 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is debated whether the higher number of macronarian sauropods in Tendaguru compared to diplodocoids in the Morrison Formation is due to environmental differences, such as conifer forests versus open plains.
facts.quote: The presence of a higher number of macronarian sauropods in the Tendaguru environment compared to numerous diplodocoids in the Morrison Formation may be due to previously known differences in environment, with the Tendaguru being dominated by conifer forest, and the Morrison being dominated by open plains of low-browse flora.
